Problem[edit]

Consider systems of three linear equations with unknowns , , and , where each of the coefficients is either or and the system has a solution other than . For example, one such system is with a nonzero solution of . How many such systems of equations are there? (The equations in a system need not be distinct, and two systems containing the same equations in a different order are considered different.)

Solution 2 (Intuitive, Straightforward)[edit]

Begin by adding the three equations. .

Each of the coefficients is 0 or 1, and cannot all equal 0. Notice that then, either , and the same for , and . Considering just for now, if equals to 0, then only 1 case exists. If equal to 1, then 3 cases exist. If equal to 2, then 3 cases still exist. If 3, then only 1 case exists. That is 8 total, so we have 24 total cases. Considering all 8 other viable systems (any permutation of besides ), given the possible coefficient cases here, we have possible cases.

Now, subtract the three equations.

Now, notice that , and the same for and . For when , that can only happen when we have only , which is 1 way. If when , we have this can happen in two ways, some permutations (except for when ) of either , which is 3 ways total. For , there are 3 ways, those being . Finally, for , we have the case . Again 8 ways total, so times 3 is 24. When we consider this system, we only consider 6 plausible cases that do not degenerate into . To see where 6 comes from; due to subtraction, if , then subtracting will yield regardless, unlike the first case, where there could exist some or not necessarily equal to 0 but add to 0 that will still satisfy. Due to properties of subtraction, that is simply impossible for three distinct equations. So, all such equations must not contain any opposites of one another. Any subset from of three elements not consisting of both and are viable roots. That is cases. Only one fifth of these are viable as four fifths pertain values that will subtract to 0, a contradiction from the first claim (particularly, casework will show that, on , , , , which is pertained by of the total will not work), so only 6 systems are valid. Therefore, we have possible solutions.

Now, the two forgotten solutions. When we add these two equations, we forget the case of redundancy (as we always count viable solutions, not infinite). When an equation is redundant, we must be able to deduce a viable ordered pair, which is the same as saying we must have systems in which their coefficients are of different parity. That is 2 cases. This however never applies for subtraction, as even if two equations have different parity, when we subtract the equations, that parity becomes constant, and will always cancel to 0, yielding only one possible solution, , which is not allowed.

So, exactly solutions are viable

Solution 3 (Solution 8 Alternate, Slightly Easier)[edit]

We proceed with casework. The following will hold if

Case 1: At least one system has , in which through the compliment, we have ways.

Case 2: Exactly two equations are equal, in which we have ways.

Case 3: An equation is the result of the sum of the other two. The equation must have some coefficients between 0 and 1, so the possible cases for the coefficients of the third equation (excluding all 0 as that has already been counted) is or permutations, or permutations, and . The first case has 0 ways. The second has 2 cases per each of the three cases, which is 6 ways total. The third has 6 cases in all, either the first equation is or some permutation (3 ways) which uniquely determines the second, or is (0,1,1) or some permutation (3 ways) which uniquely determines the second. So, there are total cases.

Case 4: All 3 are equal (except all 0, as already counted). That is 7 ways.

So, exactly cases exist.

Solution 4[edit]

Let V represent an equation in the system with variables. There are total possible systems (each coefficient can either be or ). We will subtract off the invalid ones (the equations with solution ) using casework.

We have case of selecting a 3-variable, 2-variable, and 1-variable equation, cases of selecting two -variable equations and one different -variable equation, and cases of selecting 3 of the same -variable equations. However, we can't pick two 3-variable equations in our system because then it's impossible to get to the solution So there are invalid cases. Then we need to look for a total of different cases. (Doing this beforehand makes sure we don’t accidentally skip a case.)

Case 1: 3V-2V-2V: WLOG say we have , , and . We are choosing two variables out of the 3 to be in the second equation, and we have 1 choice for the third. There are 6 ways to rearrange them. In total we get systems for this case.

Case 2: 1V-1V-1V: When we have , , and . There are 6 systems for this case.

Case 3: 2V-1V-1V: We have 3 choices for the first equation: , , or . WLOG if is the first equation, the second equation can either be or , and the third equation must be . So we have 2 choices for the second equation and 1 choice for the third. gives us 36 systems for this case.

Case 4: 3V-2V-1V: There is obviously one choice for the first equation (). For the second equation, we can choose any 2 of the 3 variables (in 3 ways). For the third, we must choose one of the two variables we included in our second equation (in 2 ways). In total, we get systems for this case.

Case 5: 2V-2V-2V: There is only 1 combination of equations: , , and . These can be rearranged in 6 ways, giving us 6 systems.

Case 6: 3V-1V-1V: Again, there's only one choice for the first equation (). For the second and third, we can choose any two of the three variables in 3 ways, giving us systems.

Case 7: 2V-2V-1V: We want to choose a variable to appear twice in both of the two variable equations. This can be done in 3 ways. The second equation will be the variable appearing twice added to the variable left out of the first (so only 1 choice), and 3 choices for the one variable equation. The system can be rearranged in 6 ways. This gives us systems.

Solution 6 (Complementary Counting)[edit]

The total number of possible systems is , with possible sets of coefficients per equation. We will use complementary counting to find the number of systems which only have the solution and subtract that from the total. Similar to what is observed in Solution 3, if any equation is repeated or , there will only be two or fewer equations for three variables, making one unique solution impossible. Therefore, we must choose different equations from possible ones, giving systems. However, there are two exceptions to consider, which will have more than one solution. The first is of the form , , ; the second is of the form , , . In both cases, there are ways to choose the variables in the equations, and then ways to arrange them, giving exceptions. Subtracting this gives systems with only one solution, and the answer is then .

~phillipzeng

Solution 7 (Complementary Counting, Linear Dependence, Vector Analysis)[edit]

Denote vector for . Thus, we need to count how many vector tuples are linearly dependent.

We do complementary counting.

First, the total number of vector tuples is .

Second, we count how many many vector tuples are linearly independent.

To meet this condition, no vector can be a zero vector .

Next, we do the casework analysis.

Case : Three vectors are all on axes.

In this case, the number of is .

Case : Two vectors are on axes and the third vector is not.

We construct such an instance in the following steps.

Step 1: We determine which two vectors lie on axes.

The number of ways is .

Step 2: For two vectors selected in Step 1, we determine which two axes they lie on.

The number of ways is .

Step 3: For the third unselected vector, we determine its value.

To make three vectors linear independent, the third vector cannot be on the plane formed by the first two vectors. So the number of ways is .

Following from the rule of product, the number of in this case is .

Case : One vector is on an axis and the other two are not.

We construct such an instance in the following steps.

Step 1: We determine which vector lies on an axis.

The number of ways is .

Step 2: For the selected vector, we determine which axis it lies on.

The number of ways is .

Step 3: We determine the values of the two unselected vectors.

First, to be linearly independent, these two vectors are distinct. Second, to be linearly independent, we cannot have one vector and another one that is a diagonal vector on the plane that is perpendicular to the first selected vector.

Thus, the number or ways in this step is .

Following from the rule of product, the number of in this case is .

Case : No vector is on any axis.

In this case, any three distinct vectors are linearly independent. So the number of in this case is .

Putting all cases together, the number of vector tuples that are linearly independent is ~Steven Chen (Professor Chen Education Palace, www.professorchenedu.com)

Solution 8 (Casework, but more intuitive)[edit]

Case 1: At least one of the equations is . By complementary counting, there are possible systems which satisfy this condition.

Case 2: Exactly 2 of the equations are equal. By directly counting, we have , where there is places to put the two identical equations, and ways to choose the nonzero equations.

Case 3: The sum of two different equations is equal to the last equation. The equation which serves as the total sum of the other two can either be which each have way respectively to pick a set of equations, and has ways to pick a set of equations. Then, we have for this case accounting for permutations.

Case 4: All 3 of the equations are equal. There are systems which satisfy this case (they cannot all be because it's already counted in Case 1).

Thus, there are total ways to pick such a system.
